result:
REST. 

Public API → unknown clients, so what matters is cacheability, predictable cost, and low onboarding friction, and REST wins all three. HTTP caching/CDN works out of the box (GraphQL: POST to one endpoint → needs persisted queries to cache). Rate limiting is per-endpoint, not query-cost analysis; arbitrary client queries → depth/complexity limits and N+1 protection are mandatory work in GraphQL. Every language has curl-level tooling, OpenAPI gives generated SDKs and docs, and status codes carry errors (GraphQL: errors usually arrive as 200 with an `errors` array → breaks naive monitoring and client handling).

GraphQL's real advantages: client picks fields → no over/underfetching, one round trip for nested data, typed schema with introspection, additive evolution with field deprecation instead of versions. These pay off when clients are varied, UI-driven, and data is a deep graph (GitHub, Shopify). They mostly benefit first-party frontends; third-party integrators typically want a few stable resources and webhooks.

Pick GraphQL instead only if consumers will build rich UIs over heavily relational data and you can staff query-cost limiting. Otherwise ship REST + OpenAPI, cursor pagination, sparse fieldsets (`?fields=`) and `?expand=` for the overfetching cases; add GraphQL later on top if demand appears, since the reverse migration is harder.
